summary_plain: The DAFT investigations tested whether a modified smoke and particle counter could operate reliably in microgravity aboard the International Space Station. Researchers used aerosol dust and cabin air to evaluate how well the device performed compared to ground tests and control instruments. This research is important for ensuring accurate smoke and fire detection systems for future space missions.
summary_expert: The Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT / DAFT-2, PSI-47) evaluated the microgravity functionality of a modified TSI P-Trak condensation nuclei counter intended for use in the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME). The modified P-Trak utilized capillary forces in the condenser tube to recycle isopropyl alcohol and omitted the orientation-detecting mercury switch. Testing involved aerosol generation using Arizona Road Dust (ARD) entrained with ISS GN2 in 15-liter Mylar bags, particulate generation from Velcro mating and de-mating, and sampling of ISS cabin air. The modified P-Trak and DustTrak control gathered data across multiple planned test points, demonstrating normal operation without clogging or optical chamber obstruction, though on-orbit count-to-mass ratios differed from ground tests due to the lack of gravitational settling for larger particles.

key_findings.text: The modified TSI P-Trak and DustTrak responded well to Velcro dust, yielding readings up to the middle of their operational ranges without error codes or zeroes, and without observed anomalies indicating normal functionality.

On-orbit flight data clustered in a region where the count-to-mass ratio was lower than determined from ground testing, indicating that without gravity to drive settling, more larger particles from the dust sample remained entrained.

Testing showed that under some circumstances, especially when significant amounts of larger ARD particles were sent to the devices, particle buildup could occur within the optics chamber of the P-Trak.
